Chapter 7. The Restructuring of Society—Family, Gender, and Education.
Now that we've explored the leadership model, let's take a closer look at how this movement reaches into the heart of everyday life. It's not just about politics—its vision stretches all the way into our homes, our schools, and even our basic ideas about family and gender.
The family, in this system, isn't just a private matter—it’s the foundation of the entire nation. Think of it as a tiny reflection of society as a whole. Traditional roles are front and center: men are expected to be providers and defenders, while women are celebrated as mothers and caretakers. The well-being of the nation is tied directly to how many children families have, and how stable those families are.
To push these ideals, a whole set of policies comes into play. Families with lots of children might get financial help or even public recognition. Marriage is strongly encouraged, and divorce? That's really frowned upon, especially for those considered most valuable to the nation. There's also a big push to keep women focused on motherhood and homemaking, rather than public life or careers.
Education gets a complete overhaul, too. It's seen as a way to shape loyalty and character from a young age. The curriculum is shifted to highlight physical fitness, military drills, and a steady stream of ideology. History and literature classes? They're rewritten to paint the nation’s past in the brightest possible light and to fire up a sense of purpose.
Imagine a typical school day starting with group exercises, patriotic songs, and lessons all about obedience and sacrifice. There’s not much room for questioning or creativity; instead, kids do a lot of memorization and work together in groups. Teachers aren’t chosen for their expertise, but for how loyal they are to the movement.
All of this is justified as crucial for the nation’s survival. The message is clear: only a disciplined, unified, and “pure” population will be strong enough to face whatever comes next. If someone dares to question this approach, or doesn’t quite fit in, they’re pushed aside or even punished—their voices are seen as dangerous.
The end result? People’s identities become tightly wrapped up in their role within the family and the nation. Personal dreams and ambitions take a back seat to the needs of the larger group. And above all, fitting in and following the rules is what gets rewarded.
